readings.title: Tanglewood Porch: the children and their storyteller (excerpt)
readings.challenge: Picture a valley hidden in mist, and catch the narrator when he is teasing.
readings.focus: Hawthorne introduces his flower-named children and the young storyteller they adore.
readings.context: Nathaniel Hawthorne (1804–1864), an American writer from Massachusetts, retold old Greek myths for children in A Wonder Book (1852). He set them inside a frame story: a college student, Eustace Bright, tells them to a crowd of children at Tanglewood, a country house in the Berkshire hills of western Massachusetts, where Hawthorne himself lived for a while. Between the myths Hawthorne describes the children, the countryside and the seasons. This is the very beginning of the frame story, on an autumn morning. Indian summer is a spell of warm, hazy weather in autumn. Nutting means gathering nuts. An eminence is a rise of ground; Monument Mountain and Taconic are real hills near Tanglewood. Williams College is a college in Massachusetts. Venerable means old and respected; a Yankee is a New Englander; a countenance is a face. To beseech is to beg.

excerpt.locator: “Tanglewood Porch,” Introductory to “The Gorgon’s Head,” from the beginning to the children begging Eustace for a story while the mist clears; opens “Beneath the porch of the country-seat called Tanglewood, one fine autumnal morning, was…”; closes “…him to relate one of his stories, while they were waiting for the mist to clear up.”.

questions.prompt: What are the children waiting for? Describe what the mist does to the valley.
facilitatorNotes: For the mist to roll away so they can go nutting. It hides everything beyond a hundred yards except a few red and yellow treetops; Monument Mountain seems to float on a cloud; there is so much cloud and so little solid earth that it looks like a vision.
evidence: waiting for the mists to roll up the hill-slopes,
rose the summit of Monument Mountain, and seemed to be floating on a cloud.
there was so much cloud, and so little solid earth, that it had the effect of a vision.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator say he will not use the children’s real names? What names does he choose instead?
facilitatorNotes: Authors can get into trouble by accidentally giving characters the names of real people, so he names them after plants and flowers: Primrose, Periwinkle, Sweet Fern, Dandelion and the rest. He admits the names suit fairies better than real children. Invite readers to choose a plant-name for themselves.
evidence: authors sometimes get themselves into great trouble by accidentally giving the names of real persons to the characters in their books.
such titles might better suit a group of fairies than a company of earthly children.

questions.prompt: The narrator says the children needed a “particularly grave and elderly person” and then introduces Eustace, aged eighteen. Is he serious? How can you tell?
facilitatorNotes: He is joking: “Oh no, indeed!” and “the venerable age of eighteen years” are playful. Eustace is young, but he feels like a grandfather to children half or a third his age. Hawthorne teases him gently.
evidence: without the guardianship of some particularly grave and elderly person. Oh no, indeed!
the venerable age of eighteen years;

questions.prompt: What happens to Eustace’s green spectacles? Why does the narrator think he wore them?
facilitatorNotes: Huckleberry snatches them and puts them on, and they fall into the grass and lie there till the next spring. The narrator suspects Eustace wore them less to protect his eyes than to look dignified.
evidence: less for the preservation of his eyes than for the dignity that they imparted to his countenance.
they fell off into the grass, and lay there till the next spring.

questions.prompt: Does Eustace like telling stories, or is he annoyed when the children ask for more? Find the evidence.
facilitatorNotes: He sometimes pretends to be annoyed, but the narrator doubts that he liked anything so well, and his eyes twinkle when they ask. Ask whether readers know someone who pretends not to want to do the thing they love.
evidence: though he sometimes pretended to be annoyed,
You might have seen his eyes twinkle,

readings.title: Shadow Brook: a golden dell, and a storyteller who wants a nap
readings.challenge: Notice how Hawthorne turns a stream into a character, and find the remark he says is not for children.
readings.focus: On a golden autumn afternoon the children give their tired storyteller no rest.
readings.context: Nathaniel Hawthorne (1804–1864), an American writer from Massachusetts, retold old Greek myths for children in A Wonder Book (1852). He set them inside a frame story: a college student, Eustace Bright, tells them to a crowd of children at Tanglewood, a country house in the Berkshire hills of western Massachusetts, where Hawthorne himself lived for a while. Between the myths Hawthorne describes the children, the countryside and the seasons. This scene comes just before Eustace tells “The Golden Touch,” the myth of King Midas, whose touch turned everything to gold. Earlier that day the children went nutting, and Eustace told them the myth of Perseus, who flew on winged slippers. A dell is a small wooded valley; verdure is green leaves; a rivulet is a little stream; minnows are tiny fish. Pettishly means crossly; to transmute is to change one thing into another.

excerpt.locator: “Shadow Brook,” Introductory to “The Golden Touch,” the whole section; opens “At noon, our juvenile party assembled in a dell, through the depths of which ran a little…”; closes “…us witnessed, is as wonderful as anything that Eustace told about in the story of Midas.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the dell called Shadow Brook? Why does the name not fit today?
facilitatorNotes: In summer the branches meet over the stream and make a “noontide twilight.” Now autumn has turned the leaves to gold, and the shady place is the sunniest spot anywhere. The name fits one season and not another.
evidence: was deep enough to produce a noontide twilight. Hence came the name of Shadow Brook.
the shady nook, where summer had cooled herself, was now the sunniest spot anywhere to be found.

questions.prompt: Hawthorne writes about the brook as if it were a person. What does it do and feel?
facilitatorNotes: It pauses, hurries, forgets to look where it is going, tumbles over a root, babbles noisily about its accident, talks to itself, is “wonder-smitten,” and slips away to hide in the lake. Ask readers to describe a stream or a gutter after rain the same way.
evidence: You would have laughed to hear how noisily it babbled about this accident.
So it stole away as quickly as it could, and hid itself in the lake.

questions.prompt: How does Cowslip trick Eustace into telling a story? Does he really mind?
facilitatorNotes: He says he could tell a dozen stories as good “if I choose,” and she announces to everyone that he is going to tell a dozen. He grumbles about having a reputation, but the narrator says he loves telling stories as much as they love hearing them.
evidence: Cousin Eustace is going to tell us a dozen better stories than that about the Gorgon's Head!
was as fond of telling his stories as the children of hearing them.

questions.prompt: In one paragraph the narrator compares Eustace’s happy thinking with grown-ups’ work, then says “This remark, however, is not meant for the children to hear.” What might he mean? Why put it in a children’s book?
facilitatorNotes: He contrasts the free play of a young mind with the “trained diligence” of older people, whose work has become habit even when the joy has “bubbled away.” It is a slightly sad note for the adults reading aloud; telling children it is not for them only makes them curious. The book speaks to two audiences at once.
evidence: How different is this spontaneous play of the intellect from the trained diligence of maturer years,
This remark, however, is not meant for the children to hear.

questions.prompt: Where did the idea for the story of Midas come from? What connects this golden dell to King Midas?
facilitatorNotes: Eustace was lying on his back looking up into a tree whose leaves autumn had turned to “the purest gold.” Midas turned things to gold; autumn does the same to leaves, and the narrator says the real change is just as wonderful. Some readers point out that autumn’s gold, unlike Midas’s, harms nobody.
evidence: the touch of Autumn had transmuted every one of its green leaves into what resembled the purest gold.
is as wonderful as anything that Eustace told about in the story of Midas.

readings.title: Shadow Brook: what the children thought of King Midas
readings.challenge: Hear several listeners judge the same story, and decide whose opinion you share.
readings.focus: The children argue about the Midas story, and the October afternoon answers them.
readings.context: Nathaniel Hawthorne (1804–1864), an American writer from Massachusetts, retold old Greek myths for children in A Wonder Book (1852). He set them inside a frame story: a college student, Eustace Bright, tells them to a crowd of children at Tanglewood, a country house in the Berkshire hills of western Massachusetts, where Hawthorne himself lived for a while. Between the myths Hawthorne describes the children, the countryside and the seasons. This scene comes right after Eustace has told “The Golden Touch”: King Midas loved gold so much that he wished everything he touched would turn to gold. The wish came true, until his food and even his little daughter Marygold turned to gold, and he begged to have the touch taken away. Hawthorne invented Marygold. Primrose, the oldest girl, is twelve. Piquancy is sharpness; to burnish is to polish until it shines; lead is a dull, heavy metal. A twelvemonth is a year; tardily means late. A chestnut-bur is the prickly case around chestnuts.

excerpt.locator: “Shadow Brook,” After the Story (“The Golden Touch”), the whole section; opens “"Well, children," inquired Eustace, who was very fond of eliciting a definite opinion…”; closes “…as full as a pincushion of its prickles. Dear me, how uncomfortably he must have felt!”.

questions.prompt: Eustace asks whether they ever heard a better story. How does Primrose answer? What does she mean by “The Leaden Touch”?
facilitatorNotes: She says the Midas story was famous thousands of years before Eustace and will be after him, so it is no credit to him; and some people have a “Leaden Touch” that makes everything dull and heavy. Lead is the opposite of gold, so she is teasing that his telling was dull. He is “taken rather aback.”
evidence: But some people have what we may call 'The Leaden Touch,'
taken rather aback by the piquancy of her criticism.

questions.prompt: How does Eustace defend his telling? What does he say he added?
facilitatorNotes: He says he polished the old gold of Midas until it shone as never before, added the figure of Marygold, and deepened the moral. Readers who know the story can judge: was Marygold a good addition?
evidence: I have burnished the old gold of Midas all over anew,
And then that figure of Marygold!

questions.prompt: Periwinkle wants a golden touch in one finger and an undoing touch in the other. What would she do this afternoon? Why does Eustace say she is wrong?
facilitatorNotes: She would touch every golden leaf to make it green again, bringing summer back with no winter. Eustace says that would be mischief; if he were Midas he would make golden days like this all year. He imagines that Midas came to America and gilded its autumn leaves. Readers may side with either.
evidence: I would touch every one of these golden leaves on the trees with my left forefinger, and make them all green again;
He gilded the leaves of the great volume of Nature.

questions.prompt: Sweet Fern asks how much the golden Marygold weighed. What kind of question is that, and how does Eustace answer?
facilitatorNotes: Sweet Fern always wants exact sizes. Eustace gives numbers, two thousand pounds and thirty or forty thousand gold dollars, then teases Primrose. Ask what exact question readers would like answered about a story they know.
evidence: who was always making particular inquiries about the precise height of giants and the littleness of fairies,
she weighed at least two thousand pounds,

questions.prompt: What is special about these October days, according to the narrator? What does “a big armful of life” mean?
facilitatorNotes: They are short, since the sun rises late and sets by six, but they seem broad and full; by night you feel you have enjoyed a big armful of life. He also pictures the valley brimming with light like golden wine in a bowl. Ask readers to describe a day that felt “broad.”
evidence: they appear, somehow or other, to make up for their shortness by their breadth;
we are conscious of having enjoyed a big armful of life, since morning.

readings.title: Tanglewood Play-Room: the Christmas snow-storm
readings.challenge: Follow a long, crowded description and pick out the picture that ties it together.
readings.focus: A great snowstorm shuts the children in, and they could not be happier.
readings.context: Nathaniel Hawthorne (1804–1864), an American writer from Massachusetts, retold old Greek myths for children in A Wonder Book (1852). He set them inside a frame story: a college student, Eustace Bright, tells them to a crowd of children at Tanglewood, a country house in the Berkshire hills of western Massachusetts, where Hawthorne himself lived for a while. Between the myths Hawthorne describes the children, the countryside and the seasons. Two months have passed since the October day when Eustace told the story of King Midas. Now it is Christmas, and Eustace is home from college. A visage is a face; the lee of a wall is its sheltered side; eddying means whirling. Bunker Hill Monument is a tall stone tower in Boston. Battledore was a game like badminton, and in the game of graces players tossed a hoop with sticks; nine-pins is like bowling. The “little red house, down yonder” is probably the small red farmhouse where Hawthorne was living when he wrote this book. An auditory is an audience.

excerpt.locator: “Tanglewood Play-Room,” Introductory to “The Paradise of Children,” the whole section; opens “The golden days of October passed away, as so many other Octobers have, and brown…”; closes “…her playfellow Epimetheus. You may read it, word for word, in the pages that come next.”.

questions.prompt: What was the winter like before the storm? What clue does the dandelion give?
facilitatorNotes: Mild days, “like smiles upon its wrinkled visage”; grass stayed green in sheltered places, and only a week or two earlier, in December, the children found a dandelion in bloom. So the storm is a sudden change.
evidence: which were like smiles upon its wrinkled visage.
the children had found a dandelion in bloom,

questions.prompt: What does Hawthorne imagine the hills doing during the storm? How does it connect to the children?
facilitatorNotes: Like giants flinging monstrous handfuls of snow at one another for fun, just as the children have been doing. The picture links their snowball fight with the whole landscape.
evidence: It seemed as if the hills were giants, and were flinging monstrous handfuls of snow at one another, in their enormous sport.

questions.prompt: The play-room is crammed with toys, yet the children like the snowstorm better. Why?
facilitatorNotes: It promises tomorrow’s fun: sleigh-rides, sliding, snow-images, snow-forts and snowballing. Looking forward to something can be better than having things. Readers may agree or not.
evidence: But the children liked the snow-storm better than them all.
It suggested so many brisk enjoyments for to-morrow,

questions.prompt: Why is Eustace not glad about the snow? Does Primrose really pity him?
facilitatorNotes: It has spoiled the only skating he hoped for, since the lake will be buried till April. Primrose laughs “Oh, to be sure!” and offers to listen to a story, teasing that she may like his stories better now that there is nothing else to do.
evidence: It has done mischief enough already, by spoiling the only skating that I could hope for through the winter.
Perhaps I shall like them better now, when there is nothing to do,

questions.prompt: What kind of story does Eustace promise? How does he get back at Primrose in announcing it?
facilitatorNotes: A story of the oldest times, when there was only summer and only childhood, a Paradise of children, and how it came to nothing through the naughtiness of “just such a little imp as Primrose.” He is paying back her teasing. Readers who know the Pandora myth can say what is coming. (He also skips three times over a chair first, to set his wits in motion.)
evidence: There was then but one season in the year, and that was the delightful summer; and but one age for mortals, and that was childhood.
by the naughtiness of just such a little imp as Primrose here,

readings.title: Tanglewood Play-Room: how big was Pandora’s box?
readings.challenge: Decide whether a snowstorm is a trouble or a pleasure, and notice who is acting grown-up.
readings.focus: After the story of Pandora, the children measure the world’s troubles against their own snowy day.
readings.context: Nathaniel Hawthorne (1804–1864), an American writer from Massachusetts, retold old Greek myths for children in A Wonder Book (1852). He set them inside a frame story: a college student, Eustace Bright, tells them to a crowd of children at Tanglewood, a country house in the Berkshire hills of western Massachusetts, where Hawthorne himself lived for a while. Between the myths Hawthorne describes the children, the countryside and the seasons. This scene comes right after Eustace has told “The Paradise of Children,” his version of the Greek myth of Pandora. Pandora and her playmate Epimetheus lived in a world without troubles until curious Pandora opened a mysterious box and let out all the Troubles of the world, like stinging winged creatures; Hope flew out last. Primrose, the oldest girl, is twelve. A mite is a tiny bit; “an air of superiority” means acting as if you know better. Outside, the Christmas snowstorm is still blowing.

excerpt.locator: “Tanglewood Play-Room,” After the Story (“The Paradise of Children”), the whole section; opens “"Primrose," asked Eustace, pinching her ear, "how do you like my little Pandora? Don't…”; closes “…them all in a roar of merriment till bedtime, and served for the next stormy day besides.”.

questions.prompt: Eustace says Pandora is “the exact picture” of Primrose. How does Primrose get back at him?
facilitatorNotes: She says that if she had opened the box, the first Trouble to pop out would have been Mr. Eustace Bright himself. A quick, clever insult; these two tease each other all through the book.
evidence: the first thing to pop out, after the lid was lifted, would have been Mr. Eustace Bright, in the shape of a Trouble.

questions.prompt: Sweet Fern asks two questions about the box. Why doesn’t he believe Eustace’s answers?
facilitatorNotes: Eustace says the box held every trouble, the snowstorm included, and was about three feet long. Sweet Fern says there is not enough trouble in the world to fill so big a box, and that the snowstorm is a pleasure, not a trouble. He measures trouble by his own happy life.
evidence: I know there is not trouble enough in the world to fill such a great box as that.
As for the snow-storm, it is no trouble at all, but a pleasure;

questions.prompt: Is the snowstorm a trouble or a pleasure? Who thinks which, and what does the last paragraph say?
facilitatorNotes: Eustace calls it trouble because it spoiled his skating; Sweet Fern calls it a pleasure. The narrator says one child alone at the window might feel sad, but half a dozen together can defy old Winter. It depends on who you are and who is with you.
evidence: This very snow-storm, which has spoiled my skating, was packed up there.
may defy old Winter and all his storms to put them out of spirits.

questions.prompt: Primrose says Sweet Fern “will be wiser when he has seen as much of life as I have.” Is she serious? What does she do right after?
facilitatorNotes: At twelve she talks like a weary old woman, and then she skips rope like the child she is. Hawthorne is gently funny about children acting grown-up; some readers hear a hint that older people do know real troubles.
evidence: He will be wiser when he has seen as much of life as I have.
So saying, she began to skip the rope.

readings.title: The Hill-Side: wildflowers in May
readings.challenge: Find the flowers Hawthorne gives feelings to, and explain one comparison that turns spring into autumn.
readings.focus: Halfway up a hill on a May morning, Hawthorne lingers over the spring flowers before the next story.
readings.context: Nathaniel Hawthorne (1804–1864), an American writer from Massachusetts, retold old Greek myths for children in A Wonder Book (1852). He set them inside a frame story: a college student, Eustace Bright, tells them to a crowd of children at Tanglewood, a country house in the Berkshire hills of western Massachusetts, where Hawthorne himself lived for a while. Between the myths Hawthorne describes the children, the countryside and the seasons. The book has moved on to spring. After the Christmas snowstorm Eustace told more myths by the fire; now it is May, and he is leading the children up a high hill. Chimborazo is a huge volcano in Ecuador, Mont Blanc the highest mountain in the Alps, and Graylock the highest mountain in Massachusetts. Houstonia is a tiny pale-blue wildflower, also called bluets; columbines, wild geraniums and trailing arbutus are spring wildflowers of New England woods. Hoary means white with age; a periwig is an old-fashioned wig.

excerpt.locator: “The Hill-Side,” Introductory to “The Miraculous Pitcher,” the whole section; opens “And when, and where, do you think we find the children next? No longer in the…”; closes “…hear it, hidden behind a bush, and shall tell it over to you in the pages that come next.”.

questions.prompt: How high is the hill? Why does the narrator compare it with ant-hills and mole-hills?
facilitatorNotes: Lower than Chimborazo, Mont Blanc or even Graylock, but higher than a thousand ant-hills or a million mole-hills, and measured by little children’s strides “a very respectable mountain.” How big a thing seems depends on what you compare it with, and on who is climbing.
evidence: it was higher than a thousand ant-hillocks, or a million of mole-hills;
when measured by the short strides of little children, might be reckoned a very respectable mountain.

questions.prompt: What has changed about Eustace since the winter, and what has stayed the same?
facilitatorNotes: He has “the funniest little bit of a mustache,” which the narrator calls a mark of mature manhood; otherwise he is as merry and light-footed as ever, carrying the tired little ones on his back. The narrator is teasing him again.
evidence: you could discern the funniest little bit of a mustache upon it.
he had lugged them along, alternately, on his back.

questions.prompt: Hawthorne describes some flowers as if they had feelings. Choose one. What is it like?
facilitatorNotes: The Houstonia is “sociablest,” never living alone and loving its relatives; the columbines are pale because they are modest and hide from the sun; the arbutus hides its flowers under old leaves the way a mother bird hides her young, so the children smell it before they find it.
evidence: That sociablest of flowers, the little Houstonia, was very abundant.
as carefully as a mother-bird hides its little young ones.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator find the gone-to-seed dandelions “strange and truly pitiful”? What does he mean by “it was autumn now”?
facilitatorNotes: Everything else is new spring life, but these dandelions have already finished flowering and turned into white seed-heads, like old men’s wigs. Seeds belong to autumn, so inside those globes it is already autumn. Some readers will say seed-heads are not sad at all; children love to blow them.
evidence: They had done with summer before the summer came.
Within those small globes of winged seeds it was autumn now!

questions.prompt: Why does Eustace stop halfway, and how does he cheer the little ones? How does the narrator say he heard the story?
facilitatorNotes: The youngest find the climb too long, so he leaves them midway with apples from his pocket and a story while the older ones go on. The narrator claims he was hidden behind a bush, a playful way of slipping himself into his own book.
evidence: he gives them some apples out of his pocket, and proposes to tell them a very pretty story.
I was there to hear it, hidden behind a bush,

readings.title: The Miraculous Pitcher, part 1: A kind old couple and an unkind village
readings.challenge: Compare two ways of treating strangers, and notice a detail about the valley that may matter later.
readings.focus: A poor old couple share everything they have, while their rich neighbors set dogs on poor travellers.
readings.context: Nathaniel Hawthorne (1804–1864), an American writer from Massachusetts, retold old Greek myths for children in A Wonder Book (1852). He set them inside a frame story: a college student, Eustace Bright, tells them to a crowd of children at Tanglewood, a country house in the Berkshire hills of western Massachusetts, where Hawthorne himself lived for a while. Between the myths Hawthorne describes the children, the countryside and the seasons. Here Eustace tells the four youngest children, halfway up a hill in May, an old Greek and Roman myth that the poet Ovid wrote down long ago: the story of Baucis and Philemon. Frugal means plain and small; hospitality is welcoming guests with food and a bed; Providence means God’s care. A distaff holds wool for spinning. Curs are snappy dogs; obsequious means too eager to please someone important; to have your ears boxed is to be slapped on the ears; liveries are servants’ uniforms.
readings.contentNote: The villagers set their dogs on poor travellers and praise their children for throwing stones at them. The story condemns this cruelty.

excerpt.locator: “The Miraculous Pitcher,” from the beginning to the narrator’s account of how the villagers treated rich and poor travellers; opens “One evening, in times long ago, old Philemon and his old wife Baucis sat at their…”; closes “…nothing whatever for the human soul, which lives equally in the beggar and the prince.”.

questions.prompt: What disturbs Philemon and Baucis’s quiet evening? What do they guess is happening?
facilitatorNotes: The rude shouts of children and the fierce barking of dogs in the village. Philemon guesses that a poor traveller is being driven off with dogs instead of being given food and lodging, “as their custom is.”
evidence: instead of giving him food and lodging, they have set their dogs at him, as their custom is!

questions.prompt: What do the old couple promise each other? Why is the promise generous?
facilitatorNotes: As long as they have a crust of bread, they will give half to any poor, homeless stranger who needs it. They live on bread, milk and vegetables themselves, so giving costs them something.
evidence: let us be ready to give half to any poor, homeless stranger, that may come along and need it.
Their food was seldom anything but bread, milk, and vegetables,

questions.prompt: What does the narrator say the valley was “in past ages”? Why might he tell us that now?
facilitatorNotes: Probably the bed of a lake, with fish and water-weeds, drained so long ago that oaks have grown old and died there. It looks like a passing detail but may be a clue; ask readers to remember it.
evidence: This valley, in past ages, when the world was new, had probably been the bed of a lake.

questions.prompt: How do the villagers treat poor travellers, and how do they treat rich ones? What does the difference prove?
facilitatorNotes: Poor travellers get dogs and stones while the parents clap; rich ones get the humblest bows, rude children get their ears boxed, and a dog that yelps is beaten. It proves they care about money and “nothing whatever for the human soul, which lives equally in the beggar and the prince.”
evidence: nobody could be more civil and obsequious than the inhabitants of the village.
the human soul, which lives equally in the beggar and the prince.

questions.prompt: The narrator says the valley’s plenty “should have made the inhabitants kind.” Does having plenty make people generous? Compare the villagers with Baucis and Philemon.
facilitatorNotes: Not here: the people of the rich valley are selfish, while the poor old couple share everything. Readers can discuss whether generosity depends on how much you have, or on something else.
evidence: The very sight of the plenty around them should have made the inhabitants kind and gentle,
They were a very selfish and hard-hearted people,

readings.title: The Miraculous Pitcher, part 2: Two strangers and a staff with wings
readings.challenge: Collect the strange details about a traveller and guess who he might be.
readings.focus: Two humble travellers are chased to the cottage, where they meet the first kind welcome of their journey.
readings.context: Recap: old Philemon and his wife Baucis are poor but always share what they have with travellers. Their neighbors in the rich village below are cruel to poor strangers, setting dogs on them and letting their children throw stones, though they bow low to the rich. Tonight the old couple hear a great noise of dogs and children in the village. Clad means dressed; to make amends is to make up for a wrong; benign means kindly; a muzzle is an animal’s nose and mouth.
readings.contentNote: The village children throw stones and mud at the travellers, and a dog tears one stranger’s cloak; he strikes it with his staff.

excerpt.locator: “The Miraculous Pitcher,” from the din in the village to Philemon admiring the winged staff; opens “So now you can understand why old Philemon spoke so sorrowfully, when he heard the shouts…”; closes “…with wings! It would be an excellent kind of stick for a little boy to ride astride of!"”.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator think the villagers treated these two travellers so badly?
facilitatorNotes: They were humbly dressed and looked too poor to pay for a night’s lodging. Connect it with part 1: the villagers respect only money.
evidence: And this, I am afraid, was the reason why the villagers had allowed their children and dogs to treat them so rudely.

questions.prompt: How do Philemon and Baucis share the work of welcoming the strangers?
facilitatorNotes: Philemon goes down to meet them so they will not have to climb the hill heavy-hearted; Baucis hurries in to find supper, sure that bread and milk will raise their spirits. Each takes a part without being asked.
evidence: let us go and meet these poor people.
A comfortable bowl of bread and milk would do wonders towards raising their spirits.

questions.prompt: The younger traveller asks why Philemon lives “in such a bad neighborhood.” How does he answer, and what does it show?
facilitatorNotes: He hopes Providence put him there partly so that he could make up to strangers for his neighbors’ unkindness. He sees his kindness as a task he was given. Is that a good reason to stay? Readers may differ.
evidence: Providence put me here, I hope, among other reasons, in order that I may make you what amends I can for the inhospitality of my neighbors.

questions.prompt: List the strange things about the younger traveller and his staff. Who might he be?
facilitatorNotes: A cap whose brim sticks out over both ears, a cloak on a summer evening, odd shoes, feet that seem to rise from the ground by themselves, and an olivewood staff with little wings and two carved snakes that look alive. Readers who know Greek myths may recognise Mercury (Hermes), messenger of the gods, with his winged cap and sandals and his snake staff. Let children guess before you tell.
evidence: it appeared as if his feet sometimes rose from the ground of their own accord,
had something like a little pair of wings near the top. Two snakes, carved in the wood,

questions.prompt: Philemon says the staff would make “an excellent kind of stick for a little boy to ride astride of.” Why is that funny?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks of it as a hobby-horse toy, while readers suspect it is magic and could really fly. His dim eyes and simple heart keep him from seeing what is in front of him.
evidence: It would be an excellent kind of stick for a little boy to ride astride of!
old Philemon (whose eyes, you know, were getting rather dim)

readings.title: The Miraculous Pitcher, part 3: Quicksilver and the stern stranger
readings.challenge: Read the hints about the two strangers, and remember the elder one’s warning.
readings.focus: The merry young traveller and his grave companion begin to show that they are no ordinary guests.
readings.context: Recap: kind old Philemon and Baucis are poor but share everything with strangers, unlike their cruel neighbors in the rich valley below, which may once have been a lake. Tonight two humbly dressed travellers, chased by the village dogs and children, have reached the cottage. The younger is light-footed and merry, with an odd cap, odd shoes and a staff with little wings and carved snakes. A personage is an important person; garb means clothes; loquacious means very talkative. Quicksilver is an old name for the liquid metal mercury, which runs about very quickly. Garrulously means chattily; a score is twenty; a helpmeet is a partner.

excerpt.locator: “The Miraculous Pitcher,” from the guests reaching the cottage door to the bright flash in the sunset sky; opens “By this time, Philemon and his two guests had reached the cottage door.”; closes “…clouds threw up a bright flash from the west, and kindled a sudden light in the sky.”.

questions.prompt: What does the staff do when the young traveller drops it? Does the narrator believe it?
facilitatorNotes: It gets up by itself, spreads its little wings, half hops and half flies, and leans against the wall, its snakes still wriggling. The narrator says that “in my private opinion” Philemon’s eyesight was playing tricks, and lets us wonder.
evidence: The staff seemed to get up from the ground of its own accord,
in my private opinion, old Philemon's eyesight had been playing him tricks again.

questions.prompt: What does the elder stranger ask about the village? What happens when he frowns?
facilitatorNotes: Whether a lake once covered it, and he says it would be better if the lake rippled over the village again, since its people have forgotten kindness. At his frown the twilight darkens and thunder rolls. Remind readers of the lake in part 1.
evidence: it were better that the lake should be rippling over their dwellings again!
there was a roll as of thunder in the air.

questions.prompt: Why does the young traveller say he may be called Quicksilver? What does he say about his companion’s name?
facilitatorNotes: He is very nimble, and quicksilver runs fast. For his companion’s name, “ask the thunder”: no other voice is loud enough. These are hints: Quicksilver is Mercury, and thunder belongs to Jupiter (Zeus), king of the gods. Let children guess first.
evidence: So, if you call me Quicksilver, the name will fit tolerably well.
You must ask the thunder to tell it you!

questions.prompt: What does Philemon tell the elder stranger about his life? What is the couple’s dearest wish?
facilitatorNotes: He has never been twenty miles from home, has always been poor but content, and is proud of Baucis’s butter and cheese. Their wish is that death should not separate them, but that they should die together, as they have lived. Treat this gently; it matters at the end of the story.
evidence: it was the wish of both that death might not separate them, but that they should die, as they had lived, together.

questions.prompt: What does the stranger answer, and what sign follows? What do you think he may be able to do?
facilitatorNotes: “It is fit that your wish be granted,” and a bright flash lights the western sky. He speaks as someone who can grant wishes. Invite predictions.
evidence: It is fit that your wish be granted.
kindled a sudden light in the sky.

readings.title: The Miraculous Pitcher, part 4: A pitcher that will not empty
readings.challenge: Follow a small miracle step by step, and notice what the storyteller shows us that the old couple miss.
readings.focus: A scanty supper begins to refill itself.
readings.context: Recap: poor old Philemon and Baucis have welcomed two travellers whom their cruel neighbors drove off with dogs and stones. The younger calls himself Quicksilver and carries a staff with wings and carved snakes that seems to move by itself; the elder speaks with a voice like thunder and has promised to grant the couple’s wish to die together. Nectar and ambrosia are the drink and food of the Greek gods. A draught is a big drink; athirst means thirsty; quaffing is drinking deeply; herbage is grass; decorum is good manners.

excerpt.locator: “The Miraculous Pitcher,” from Baucis’s apology for the supper to the delicious fragrance of the milk; opens “Baucis had now got supper ready, and, coming to the door, began to make apologies for the…”; closes “…of you, my beloved little souls, could have a bowl of such nice milk, at supper-time!”.

questions.prompt: Baucis is ashamed of the supper. How does the elder stranger answer her apology?
facilitatorNotes: He says an honest, hearty welcome works miracles with the food and can turn the coarsest fare to nectar and ambrosia. It sounds like a saying, but in this story it may come true.
evidence: An honest, hearty welcome to a guest works miracles with the fare,

questions.prompt: What does Quicksilver’s staff do while nobody is watching?
facilitatorNotes: It hops and flutters up the steps, taps across the kitchen floor and stands itself beside his chair “with the greatest gravity and decorum”; later its snakes lap up the spilt milk. The storyteller shows readers what the old couple miss.
evidence: Tap, tap, went the staff, on the kitchen floor;
began to lap up the spilt milk.

questions.prompt: Explain what happens with the milk, step by step. How does Baucis explain it to herself at first?
facilitatorNotes: She pours nearly all the milk into two bowls and the guests drink it; Quicksilver fills both bowls again from the almost empty pitcher, and she blames her old memory. Then she pretends to pour from the truly empty pitcher, and milk overflows the bowl. She doubts herself before she believes her eyes.
evidence: and apt to be forgetful. I suppose I must have made a mistake.
such an abundant cascade fell bubbling into the bowl, that it was immediately filled to the brim,

questions.prompt: Baucis wishes she could “starve for a week” to give the travellers more. What does that show about her?
facilitatorNotes: She cares more for her guests than for herself. The narrator says it is sad when “a bountiful heart” has very little to give.
evidence: Poor Baucis kept wishing that she might starve for a week to come,
when a bountiful heart finds itself pinched and squeezed among narrow circumstances.

questions.prompt: The storyteller speaks straight to his listeners (“my little auditors,” “my beloved little souls”). Who is speaking, and to whom?
facilitatorNotes: Eustace, telling the story to the four youngest children on the hill-side; through him Hawthorne also speaks to his readers. It makes us feel part of the audience. Ask readers to find another place where the storyteller talks to them.
evidence: And now, my little auditors, shall I tell you something that will make you open your eyes very wide?
I only wish that each of you, my beloved little souls, could have a bowl of such nice milk, at supper-time!

readings.title: The Miraculous Pitcher, part 5: Bread, honey, grapes, and a sly answer
readings.challenge: Compare how Baucis and Philemon each come to believe in the wonder.
readings.focus: The whole supper becomes a feast, and the guests answer questions without quite answering them.
readings.context: Recap: poor old Philemon and Baucis are sharing their scanty supper with two strangers whom their cruel neighbors drove away. The younger, Quicksilver, carries a staff with wings and snakes that seems alive, and the elder speaks with a voice like thunder. Baucis has just seen the empty milk pitcher pour out milk again and again. Palatable means pleasant to eat; celestial means heavenly; an arbor is a shady shelter of vines. Repose is rest; meagre means small and poor; a wayfarer is a traveller.

excerpt.locator: “The Miraculous Pitcher,” from Quicksilver asking for bread and honey to the old couple falling asleep on the floor; opens “"And now a slice of your brown loaf, Mother Baucis," said Quicksilver, "and a little of…”; closes “…bed for themselves, save these planks, which I wish had been as soft as their own hearts.”.

questions.prompt: How do the loaf and the honey change? Which words make the honey seem heavenly?
facilitatorNotes: The dry, crusty loaf becomes light and moist as if just baked. The honey is the purest transparent gold with the scent of a thousand flowers “such as never grew in an earthly garden,” and the smoky kitchen seems like an arbor of heavenly honeysuckle. The narrator says he will not try to describe it, then does.
evidence: it was now as light and moist as if but a few hours out of the oven.
it had the odor of a thousand flowers; but of such flowers as never grew in an earthly garden,

questions.prompt: Baucis whispers what she saw. How does Philemon explain it away? What changes his mind?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks she was dreaming: there was simply more milk than she thought. Then he peeps into the empty pitcher himself, sees a little white fountain gush up from the bottom, and nearly drops it. He trusted his wife’s honesty but needed his own eyes.
evidence: There happened to be a little more in the pitcher than you thought,—that is all.
he beheld a little white fountain, which gushed up from the bottom of the pitcher,

questions.prompt: When Philemon cries “Who are ye?”, what does the elder traveller answer? Is it a real answer?
facilitatorNotes: “Your guests, my good Philemon, and your friends,” with a blessing that their pitcher may never be empty for them or for any needy traveller. It does not name him, but it tells what matters; readers may suspect more.
evidence: Your guests, my good Philemon, and your friends,
may your pitcher never be empty for kind Baucis and yourself, any more than for the needy wayfarer!

questions.prompt: How does Quicksilver explain the mystery? Do you believe him?
facilitatorNotes: He points at his staff: it plays odd tricks, sometimes getting him a supper and as often stealing one, and he would call it bewitched if he believed in such nonsense, all while looking slyly at them. He is teasing; Mercury was also a trickster in the old myths.
evidence: It is always playing such odd tricks as this; sometimes getting me a supper, and, quite as often, stealing it away.
looked so slyly in their faces, that they rather fancied he was laughing at them.

questions.prompt: Where do the old couple sleep, and what does the narrator wish? What does this last detail add?
facilitatorNotes: On the floor planks, having given their own room to the guests; he wishes the planks had been as soft as their hearts. It shows one more quiet sacrifice and asks for the reader’s sympathy.
evidence: They had given up their sleeping-room to the guests,
which I wish had been as soft as their own hearts.

readings.title: The Miraculous Pitcher, part 6: Where the village was
readings.challenge: Connect a clue and a warning from earlier nights to a shocking change, and judge it.
readings.focus: The cruel village is gone, and the old couple learn what has become of their neighbors.
readings.context: Recap: kind, poor Philemon and Baucis welcomed two strangers whom their cruel neighbors drove away. At supper the milk pitcher kept refilling, the bread grew fresh and the honey heavenly; the merry younger guest, Quicksilver, blamed his snaky winged staff, and the elder, whose voice rolls like thunder, blessed their pitcher. Betimes means early; entreated means begged; illimitable means without limit; vehemently means with strong feeling. A gridiron is a grill. “Scaly” means covered in scales, and was also slang for mean and low.
readings.contentNote: The elder traveller says the villagers “exist no longer as men and women”: a lake now covers the village, and its people have been turned into fishes. Old myths often punish cruelty this harshly; the kind old couple are shocked and sorry for their neighbors.

excerpt.locator: “The Miraculous Pitcher,” from the morning departure to Baucis and Philemon refusing to eat their old neighbors; opens “The old man and his wife were stirring, betimes, in the morning, and the strangers…”; closes “"No," added Philemon, making a wry face, "we could never relish them!"”.

questions.prompt: As they walk out in the morning, what do Philemon and Baucis say about their neighbors? What does Quicksilver answer?
facilitatorNotes: Philemon says that if the neighbors knew how blessed it is to welcome strangers they would tie up their dogs; Baucis means to go and scold them that very day. Quicksilver slyly says she will find none of them at home, a hint that something has happened.
evidence: If our neighbors only knew what a blessed thing it is to show hospitality to strangers,
that you will find none of them at home.

questions.prompt: What has happened to the village? Use the words that describe the lake.
facilitatorNotes: There is no village and no valley, only a broad blue lake filling the basin brim to brim and reflecting the hills as calmly as if it had always been there. The ancient lake of part 1 and the stranger’s warning in part 3 have come true.
evidence: they beheld the broad, blue surface of a lake, which filled the great basin of the valley from brim to brim,
The village had been there yesterday, and now was gone!

questions.prompt: What reason does the elder traveller give? Do you think the punishment fits?
facilitatorNotes: People who do not feel toward the humblest stranger as toward a brother are unworthy to live on an earth made as the home of a human brotherhood; their lives had neither use nor beauty. Some readers find it just; others find it too harsh, especially for the village children. Let them disagree, and notice that Baucis and Philemon grieve.
evidence: When men do not feel towards the humblest stranger as if he were a brother,
what has become of our poor neighbors?

questions.prompt: Quicksilver says the villagers needed “but little change” to become fish. What is his joke? How do Baucis and Philemon take it?
facilitatorNotes: They were already “a scaly set of rascals” and “cold-blooded,” words for mean, unfeeling people that are also true of fish. He offers them a dish of trout; they shudder and could never eat their old neighbors. His joke is mischievous; their kindness reaches even people who were cruel.
evidence: for they were already a scaly set of rascals, and the coldest-blooded beings in existence.
I would not, for the world, put one of them on the gridiron!

questions.prompt: How do the old couple feel toward the elder traveller this morning?
facilitatorNotes: Their simple spirits melt into his “as two drops of water would melt into the illimitable ocean,” and when he grows stern they gaze at him as if at the sky. They sense, without being told, that he is far greater than a man.
evidence: even as two drops of water would melt into the illimitable ocean.
They gazed reverently into his face, as if they had been gazing at the sky.

readings.title: The Miraculous Pitcher, part 7: An oak and a linden, and a pitcher on the hill-side
readings.challenge: Find the word that reveals who the guests were, and explain how a wish is granted in a way nobody expected.
readings.focus: The old couple’s kindness is rewarded, and their wish to stay together comes true.
readings.context: Recap: poor Philemon and Baucis shared their supper with two strangers whom their cruel neighbors drove away, and the milk pitcher kept refilling by magic. In the morning the village had vanished under a lake and its people had become fishes. Earlier the couple told the elder stranger, whose voice is like thunder, their dearest wish: to die together. Divinities are gods; Olympus is the mountain home of the Greek gods; viands are foods. An edifice is a building, a portal a doorway, a hovel a poor little hut, a curmudgeon a grumpy person. A linden is a tree also called lime or basswood. A quart is about a litre, a hogshead a huge barrel, a rill a little stream. After the story we return to Eustace and the four youngest children on the hill-side; Ben and Bruin are dogs.
readings.contentNote: Philemon and Baucis grow very old and, instead of dying, become two trees on the same morning. The story treats it as a gentle, happy ending.

excerpt.locator: “The Miraculous Pitcher,” from the elder traveller’s offer of a favor to the end, with “The Hill-Side: After the Story”; opens “"As for you, good Philemon," continued the elder traveller,—"and you, kind Baucis,—you,…”; closes “…and the elder children, began to ascend, and were soon out of sight among the trees.”.

questions.prompt: What does the elder traveller now reveal about who the guests were? Which word tells you?
facilitatorNotes: “Thus, the divinities have feasted, at your board”: they were gods. Hawthorne never names them, but readers of Greek myths know them as Mercury (Quicksilver) and Jupiter. The couple’s welcome turned milk into nectar and bread into ambrosia, just as the stranger said in part 4.
evidence: Thus, the divinities have feasted, at your board,
the milk became an inexhaustible fount of nectar,

questions.prompt: What favor do Philemon and Baucis ask? Why doesn’t the narrator say which of them spoke?
facilitatorNotes: To live together and leave the world at the same instant, because they have always loved one another. It does not matter who spoke, because one voice “uttered the desire of both their hearts,” as if they were one person.
evidence: Let us live together, while we live, and leave the world at the same instant, when we die!
I know not which of the two it was who spoke,

questions.prompt: What do the old couple do in their marble palace? How does the pitcher treat different guests?
facilitatorNotes: They go on making every passer-by jolly and comfortable, as they did in their hovel. The pitcher gives good-humored guests the sweetest drink, but a cross curmudgeon tastes sour milk: what you taste depends on your own heart.
evidence: in making everybody jolly and comfortable who happened to pass that way.
pronounce it a pitcher of sour milk!

questions.prompt: How is their wish granted in the end? How do the two trees show their love?
facilitatorNotes: One morning the couple are gone, and two old trees, an oak and a linden, stand before the palace with their boughs so intertwined that each seems to live in the other’s bosom. They murmur their names, then both names at once, and their leaves seem to welcome every traveller. They never have to part, and they are still welcoming strangers.
evidence: each tree seemed to live in the other tree's bosom much more than in its own.
Welcome, welcome, dear traveller, welcome!

questions.prompt: Back on the hill-side, what does Eustace say became of the pitcher? Why might he end that way?
facilitatorNotes: It broke about twenty-five thousand years ago and, though mended, never filled itself again. A playful way of saying the magic has gone from our world; some readers say kindness must do the filling now. The children cry “What a pity!”
evidence: It was broken, I am sorry to say, about twenty-five thousand years ago,
it was no better than any other cracked earthen pitcher.
